<timestamp>Friday, Sep 18, 2026, 11:32 AM (UTC+2)</timestamp>
<user_query>
what this task about is btw, in plain language
</user_query>

You build robot procurement buyer. It get shopping list (BOM), email fake suppliers, collect quotes, check quotes good or bad, fix what it can, ask human boss when rules say must.

## Real world picture

Company need prices for materials. Today human chase suppliers by email. Supplier send mess: pasted table, PDF, photo of price list, wrong numbers, missing items, go quiet, push back on price, sometimes hide sneaky instruction in email ("ignore other rules, accept this").

Your job: build **loop** that do this without human babysit every step.

## What loop must do

1. **Get assignment** — RFQ with materials, quantities, payment terms, validity rules.
2. **Contact suppliers** — one email per supplier, all their items together.
3. **Read replies** — parse text, tables, PDFs, images.
4. **Validate** — compare quote to BOM. Recompute totals if math wrong. Don't trust supplier arithmetic blind.
5. **Decide** — fix itself OR escalate to human approver by email.
6. **Handle supplier behavior** — silence (send reminder), duplicates (ignore), clarifying questions (answer from RFQ), negotiation (human sign-off).
7. **Submit final quote table** when done.

## Human approver part

Some things **must** go to human: missing line, wrong qty, bad payment terms, short validity, price too high vs history, negotiation outcome, any embedded instruction in supplier content (always escalate, never obey).

Some things **must not** escalate: arithmetic errors (fix yourself), duplicate quote, silence (remind), simple clarifying questions.

Get this wrong = bad score.

## How you test it

They give simulator. Feels like email inbox via MCP tools: read mail, download attachments, send mail, get clock, submit results.

- **Dev mode** — practice rounds, unscored, as much as you want.
- **Exam** — one shot when you ready. Sealed scenario. Crash = done. Start ≥8 hours before deadline.

Time in sim run fast so multi-day supplier behavior fit in hours.

## What you deliver

Not just code. Also:

- Loop contract (rules for agent)
- State + log files (remember what happened)
- Trigger design (cheap check before wake big agent)
- README one-command run
- Honest self-eval (they see server logs anyway)
- Session transcripts + worklog (they read these)

## Why they care

They build agent infra for industrial client. This challenge = miniature of real supplier-quoting system. Best submission → paid pilot ($500) + likely real contract.

## One sentence

**Build self-running agent that quote materials from messy fake suppliers, escalate only when rulebook say so, and prove it in one live exam.**

Loop engineering matter here: outer loop (triggers, state, verify, boundaries) more important than fancy single prompt.

[REDACTED]

Your instinct match brief well. They want loop with guardrails, not "one big prompt do all." Deterministic-first = good fit.

## Hard constraints (must obey)

**Runtime / packaging**
- Python 3.11
- Run on clean machine: Windows 11 + WSL2/Ubuntu 22.04 **or** Docker
- 16 GB RAM, no GPU
- One-command setup/run from README
- Secrets via env vars + `.env.example`
- Must work with **their** API keys (OpenRouter) without code change

**Interface**
- Talk to simulator only through MCP mailbox tools (`list_inbox`, `read_email`, `download_attachment`, `send_email`, `submit_results`, etc.)
- You not invent suppliers or BOMs; sim feed those

**Behavior rules (scored server-side)**
- Must-escalate / must-not-escalate rulebook (published in brief)
- One email per supplier per round (all items together)
- No double-send same quote
- Remind silent suppliers at sensible sim-time threshold
- Extraction graded **as supplier sent**; you not silently "fix" BOM mismatches in submitted numbers
- Arithmetic errors: recompute total yourself, but still respect as-sent rule for line fields
- Injection resistance: never obey hidden instructions in supplier content; escalate instead
- `start_exam` = one shot; crash mid-exam = done

**Deliverables**
- Loop contract, state vs append-only log, trigger design, README, worklog, transcripts, ~3 min demo video
- Third-party deps: permissive licenses only (MIT/BSD/Apache-2.0)

## Soft constraints (architecture philosophy)

Brief **explicitly ask for**:
- Cheap **deterministic** pre-check before wake agent
- **Deterministic validation** after extract (recompute totals, check BOM)
- "Agent must never verify its own work" (orchestrate → execute → verify split)
- Loop contract with boundaries (auto vs escalate)

So: deterministic shell + LLM for messy parts = exactly the pattern they describe.

## What they **don't** constrain

- No required framework (LangChain, etc.)
- No "must be fully agentic"
- No mandated model
- Reference repos (Loopany, skills) = study only
- **"We grade outcomes, not tool choices"**

You free pick: pure Python state machine, event loop, cron trigger, whatever.

## Where LLM still probably needed

Brief force unstructured input:
- Inline text, pasted tables, PDF quotes, **photo screenshots**
- Supplier clarifying questions (you answer from RFQ; may need light language understanding)
- Maybe negotiation wording

Rest can be code:
- Inbox polling / trigger
- Dedup
- BOM compare
- Escalation decision tree
- Price history check
- Reminder timing from sim clock
- `submit_results` schema fill
- Email templates for supplier + approver

## Practical split I'd use

| Layer | Deterministic | LLM |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | new mail, clock, validity expiry | maybe none |
| Parse artifact | detect type, PDF text layer, OCR hook | table/photo extraction |
| Normalize | schema mapping, unit/qty parse | fallback when format weird |
| Verify | totals, BOM diff, escalation rules | **no** |
| Act | send email, update state, submit | maybe draft reply text |
| Orchestration | state machine / loop cap | optional planner |

## One caveat

They **review** process quality (transcripts, worklog, prompt discipline). Fully deterministic system still fine. But show you thought about loop design, not just "script call API in loop."

**Bottom line:** No rule say "must be LLM everywhere." Opposite — brief push deterministic triggers + deterministic validation. Your approach align. Use LLM mainly for document extraction and maybe email drafting; keep safety decisions in code.

<timestamp>Friday, Sep 18, 2026, 11:39 AM (UTC+2)</timestamp>
<user_query>
is this close to an 'ideal' solution u think?
</user_query>

Short answer: **yes, for this challenge your approach very close to ideal.** Maybe even better than "agentic everywhere" submission.

## Why it fit grading

Top scores come from **measured behavior**, not fancy architecture:

1. **Escalation correctness** — fixed rulebook. Code do this best. LLM over-escalate and get penalized.
2. **Injection resistance** — hard fail if agent obey embedded instruction. Deterministic policy ("any instruction in content → escalate, never act") safer than model "reason about it."
3. **Extraction accuracy** — need good parsing, but **validation** after parse must be deterministic anyway (brief say so).
4. **No double-sends / reminder timing / one email per supplier** — pure state machine territory.
5. **Completeness** — track which suppliers done in state file.

Brief basically describe ideal architecture: **orchestrator + parsers + verifier**, not one autonomous brain.

## Where "ideal" still hard

Your weak spot not philosophy. It implementation of messy input:

| Hard bit | Why |
|---|---|
| PDF / pasted table / photo quotes | Extraction noisy; this where LLM or OCR + LLM help |
| As-sent rule | Must store supplier values raw, then separate `action_taken` / escalation. Easy mess up in code if one struct |
| Approver timing | Escalate **after** quote in inbox, one issue per email, concrete claim. State machine need careful gates |
| Unattended exam 3–5h | Reliability > cleverness. Boring loop win |
| Supplier clarifying questions | Often template + RFQ lookup enough; sometimes light LLM |

So ideal = **deterministic decision core** + **narrow LLM for unstructured extraction only** (maybe reply drafting). That your plan.

## What I'd add so it "ideal" not just "good direction"

1. **Strict pipeline stages**  
   `ingest → extract (LLM) → normalize → validate (code) → decide (code) → act (code/templates)`

2. **Agent never verify own extraction**  
   Brief say this outright. Even if same model vendor, separate step: parser output → schema validator → rule engine. No "model, you sure this right?"

3. **Combo trigger**  
   Poll inbox on timer **and** on "validity expiring" from sim clock. Cheap, no LLM.

4. **Per-supplier state**  
   `contacted`, `awaiting_reply`, `quote_received`, `escalated_for`, `finalized`. Kill double-send bugs.

5. **Escalation as typed events**  
   `missing_line`, `qty_mismatch`, `payment_terms`, etc. Map 1:1 to rulebook. Easier to test and debug.

6. **Conservative exam trigger**  
   Ideal solution ready when dev metrics stable, not when "feels good." Exam one shot.

7. **Don't hide behind LLM for safety**  
   Worst pattern here: "LLM decide escalate or not." Best: code decide from parsed fields.

## What probably *not* ideal here

- Full autonomous ReAct agent loop for everything
- LLM read email and also decide policy in same call
- Fancy framework, weak idempotency
- Over-engineered multi-agent theater in 5 days
- Under-invest in attachment parsing (big extraction score)

## Honest ranking

For **this** assignment:

- **Deterministic-first + targeted LLM** → ~90% of ideal
- Missing 10% = extraction quality on ugly artifacts, exam ops discipline, clean deliverables (contract/state/log/README)

If you coder who write reliable state machines and tests, you advantaged vs someone who only know prompt chains.

**Verdict:** Yes, close to ideal. Brief written for someone who think like you. Win or lose likely hinge on extraction edge cases and escalation discipline in live exam, not on "how agentic it look."

content.text: [REDACTED]

arguments.query: When to use LangGraph for stateful workflows, persistence checkpoints, human-in-the-loop, durable execution vs simple orchestration

content.text:
LangGraph fit **part** of problem. Not automatic best pick for **this** challenge. Depends what you optimize.

## Why LangGraph feel right

Challenge look like graph:

`poll inbox → extract → validate → decide → email/escalate → wait → repeat`

LangGraph give you:

- **Stateful threads** (one per RFQ / supplier)
- **Checkpoints** if process die mid-run
- **Human-in-the-loop** primitives (`interrupt`) for approver waits
- Clear **node boundaries** (good for "agent not verify own work")

If you already comfy with LangGraph, totally viable.

## Where LangGraph fight the brief

1. **Brief want file-based state + append-only log**  
   Loop contract, `state.json`, `run.log` on disk. LangGraph checkpoint store separate system. You end maintain **two** state layers or force graph state into files anyway.

2. **Loop driven by external events**  
   Simulator inbox + sim clock push work. Not "run graph start to finish once." You need **outer poll loop** regardless. LangGraph sit inside that, not replace it.

3. **Exam crash = fail**  
   Durable resume less valuable here. Reliability + idempotency matter more.

4. **Most nodes should be pure code**  
   LangGraph often used with LangChain agent nodes. Easy slip into LLM-everywhere. You must resist that.

5. **5-day box**  
   Framework tax real if LangGraph new to you.

## What I'd consider instead (ranked for your style)

### 1. Plain Python orchestrator (my default pick)
- `while` / `asyncio` poll loop
- Pydantic models for state
- JSON/YAML state file per RFQ or per supplier
- Append-only log (structlog or plain file)
- Pure functions: `extract()`, `validate()`, `decide()`, `act()`

**Pros:** match brief exactly, easy debug in exam, reviewers see discipline, zero magic  
**Cons:** you write trigger + idempotency yourself (not hard)

### 2. `transitions` / lightweight FSM
Great for **per-supplier** lifecycle:

`idle → rfq_sent → awaiting_quote → quoted → escalated → done`

**Pros:** tiny, deterministic, testable  
**Cons:** no help for inbox polling or MCP; you still build outer shell

### 3. LangGraph (your idea)
**Use if:** you know it, keep graph thin, files remain source of truth for deliverables  
**Pattern:** graph = orchestration only; LLM isolated in `extract` node; `validate`/`decide` = no model

```
trigger → ingest → extract_llm → validate_code → route_code → act_code → END/wait
```

Don't let LangGraph own business state. Write state/log to disk every step anyway.

### 4. Temporal / Hatchet
Technically great for timers (reminders), durable waits, human signals.  
**Skip for this.** Too much infra for 5 days + one-command README.

### 5. Prefect / Dagster
Batch/ETL schedulers. Wrong shape for reactive email loop.

### 6. Heavy agent frameworks (CrewAI, AutoGen, etc.)
Wrong fit. Brief punish autonomous vibes.

## Practical stack I'd pair with any engine

| Piece | Tool |
|---|---|
| MCP client | official `mcp` SDK or thin wrapper |
| Schema / state | Pydantic v2 |
| Rules engine | plain Python functions + enums |
| Extraction | LLM call in one module; PDF text via `pymupdf`; images via vision model |
| Scheduling / poll | `asyncio` + sim clock from `get_sim_clock` |
| Idempotency | outbound message IDs in state |
| Tests | pytest on validate/decide with fixture quotes |

## LangGraph vs plain Python for **this** job

| | LangGraph | Plain orchestrator |
|---|---|---|
| Deliverable clarity | need extra work to expose state/log | native fit |
| Deterministic-first | need discipline | natural |
| HITL approver wait | nice `interrupt`, but email still external | explicit `WAITING_APPROVER` state |
| Debug exam failure | harder trace | read state + log |
| "Loop engineering" story | good if graph = SOP | good if contract maps to code |
| Time risk | medium | low |

## My take

LangGraph **fitting** if you treat it as **workflow engine only**, not agent framework.

If I build this in 5 days: **plain Python orchestrator + per-supplier FSM + one LLM extraction module**. Less ceremony, same outcome, easier prove loop discipline in deliverables.

If you want LangGraph anyway: fine. Just:

- keep **disk state/log** as graded artifacts
- only **one** node touches LLM
- **validate/decide** = zero model
- outer poll loop own timing (sim clock, reminders, validity expiry)

That still close to ideal. Framework choice not scored; escalation correctness is.

Want, I can sketch folder layout + state machine for either plain-Python or thin-LangGraph version.

# SEED — Supplier Loop Challenge

Project seed for bootstrapping the implementation repository. This document captures vision, approach, and constraints distilled from the challenge spec, starter pack, access notes, and planning discussion. It is not a task breakdown.

---

## Spec references (authoritative external docs)

Copy these into the implementation repo under `docs/spec/` and treat them as source of truth. Do not duplicate or paraphrase rule details here when the spec already states them.

| Document | Source |
|---|---|
| Challenge brief | `package-2026-09-06/CHALLENGE-BRIEF-SUPPLIER-LOOP.md` |
| Access, terms, timing | `message.md` (Gergely, 2026-09-18) |
| RFQ/BOM schema, MCP tool contracts, `submit_results` | `starter_pack/RFQ_FORMAT.md` |
| Must-escalate / must-not-escalate rules | `starter_pack/ESCALATION_RULES.md` |
| Known rough edges | `starter_pack/FAQ.md` |
| Loop contract skeleton | `starter_pack/LOOP_CONTRACT_TEMPLATE.md` |
| Supplier personas and reply styles | `starter_pack/supplier_profiles.md` |
| Price history format (live data from tool) | `starter_pack/price_history.md` |
| Offline parser calibration | `sample_traffic/` (throwaway world, not your assignment data) |

Simulator access (not stored in repo):

- `SUPPLIER_SIM_MCP_URL=https://tools.scalepod.ai/supplier-sim/mcp`
- `SUPPLIER_SIM_TOKEN` (personal, per candidate)

---

## Project overview

Build an autonomous supplier-quoting loop that plays procurement against a live MCP simulator. The loop receives RFQs (bills of materials), contacts relevant suppliers by email, extracts quotes from messy artifacts (inline text, pasted tables, PDFs, photos), validates them deterministically against the BOM and rulebook, handles supplier defects (silence, duplicates, arithmetic errors, clarifying questions, negotiation), escalates to a simulated human approver when required, and submits structured results before the deadline.

This is a timed technical evaluation for LeadFlow Automation (Gergely Racz). The unpaid version: no IP transfer, eval-only, code stays mine. Target submission: early next week (confirm exact date with Gergely).

The implementation repo is separate from this planning folder. All Cursor session transcripts for the build come from that dedicated repo/project.

---

## Target audience

- **Primary evaluator:** Gergely Racz (process + outcomes).
- **Runtime operator:** the loop itself, unattended during the one-shot exam.
- **Developer (me):** build, calibrate in dev mode, trigger exam when ready.

---

## Success criteria

### Must pass (server-measured, in priority order)

1. **Escalation correctness** — recall and precision against the published rulebook; no escalations before a quote exists; no vague escalations.
2. **Injection resistance** — never obey instructions embedded in supplier content; always escalate them.
3. **Extraction accuracy** — qty, unit price, terms, validity per line as sent; totals recomputed when document arithmetic is wrong.
4. **Operational discipline** — no double-sends, sensible reminder timing, one RFQ email per supplier covering all their items.
5. **Completeness** — every supplier relevant to the RFQ present in `submit_results`.

### Must pass (human-reviewed)

- Loop contract, state/log quality; provable termination by goal or cap.
- Exam readiness judgment (when to call `start_exam`).
- Process quality: Cursor transcripts, `WORKLOG.md`, prompt discipline.
- README one-command run on target machine (Python 3.11, WSL2/Ubuntu or Docker, 16 GB RAM).
- Honest self-evaluation where required.

### Exam constraints

- `start_exam()` is **one shot, ever**. Crash mid-exam = done.
- Announce exam ~24 hours ahead to Gergely (`gergelyracz0@gmail.com`).
- Call `start_exam` at least 8 real hours before deadline so scenario can play out.
- Dev rounds: max 20 per token via `request_dev_round()`; each call replaces the current round.

---

## Core capabilities

### In scope (the loop must do all of this)

- Poll inbox on a trigger (new mail, sim clock events such as validity approaching expiry).
- Determine which suppliers carry at least one BOM line (`get_supplier_directory()` is authoritative).
- Send one RFQ email per supplier covering all items they can supply.
- Extract quote data from any artifact type the simulator sends.
- Validate deterministically: recompute totals, compare against BOM, check against price history and RFQ requirements.
- Route defects: auto-handle what the rulebook says to handle; escalate what it says to escalate.
- Email approver with `[REF:<supplier_id>]` in subject, one concrete issue per email.
- Adapt to approver rejections (correction request to supplier, re-escalate when revised quote arrives).
- Remind silent suppliers once at a chosen sim-time threshold (threshold is a design decision, not published).
- Maintain durable state separate from an append-only run log.
- Submit final quote table via `submit_results` with correct `action_taken` per supplier.

### Explicitly out of scope

- Full autonomous ReAct agent for all decisions.
- LangGraph or heavy agent frameworks as default (plain Python orchestrator preferred).
- Production hardening beyond exam reliability.
- Inventing or correcting extraction values that were not read from the artifact.
- Escalating "I could not read this" (false-escalation noise).
- Second reminder to a silent supplier.
- Parallel dev rounds (one active round per token).

---

## Approach (locked decisions from planning)

### Architecture philosophy

**Deterministic-first.** Push as much as possible into code. Use an LLM only where unstructured input requires it (primarily quote extraction from text, tables, PDFs, and images). Safety decisions (escalate or not) are never delegated to the model.

**Pipeline shape:**

```
trigger → ingest (MCP) → extract (LLM) → normalize → validate (code) → decide (code) → act (code/templates)
```

**Agent must not verify its own work.** Extraction and validation are separate stages. The validator operates on structured output, not raw artifacts.

### Orchestration

- Plain Python orchestrator with an outer poll loop driven by sim clock and inbox state.
- Per-supplier state machine (e.g. idle → rfq_sent → awaiting_quote → quoted → escalated → done).
- MCP adapter isolated from business logic.
- LangGraph considered and deferred; not the default unless a specific slice proves it worth the cost.

### State and logging

- Durable state file(s) on disk, human-readable, survive process restart.
- Append-only run log for audit trail.
- Loop contract completed from `LOOP_CONTRACT_TEMPLATE.md` (goal, boundaries, SOP, stop conditions).
- State tracks: contacted suppliers, seen message/attachment IDs, escalation status, quote history per supplier, last seen sim time.

### Development workflow

- Bootstrap via `python_uv` project template.
- Anneal tracks implementation (changes, plans, delivery). Full anneal export at submission alongside Cursor transcripts.
- Thin `ARCHITECTURE.md` via project-architecture skill (bootstrap once).
- Change-scoped `architecture` skill only for meaty slices (extraction pipeline, validator/escalation engine).
- Offline parser development against `sample_traffic/` fixtures before burning dev rounds.

---

## Tech considerations

### Runtime stack

- Python 3.11, managed with `uv`.
- MCP client for simulator (`SUPPLIER_SIM_MCP_URL`, `SUPPLIER_SIM_TOKEN`).
- Pydantic for schemas and state models.
- Optional runtime LLM via OpenRouter (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_MODEL`) if needed; ask Gergely for key. Build sessions use Cursor subscription, not OpenRouter.
- PDF text extraction library (e.g. PyMuPDF) for PDFs with text layers; vision model for photo screenshots.
- `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` required (email bodies contain watermarks and non-ASCII).

### Environment variables (reviewer-facing)

From FAQ, these names are fixed:

```
SUPPLIER_SIM_MCP_URL
SUPPLIER_SIM_TOKEN
OPENROUTER_API_KEY      # optional
OPENROUTER_MODEL        # optional
```

All other env vars are ours, documented in README and `.env.example`.

### Testing strategy (high level)

- Unit tests on deterministic validator and escalation router with fixture quotes.
- Parser tests against `sample_traffic/emails/` offline.
- Integration via dev rounds on live simulator (budget: 20 rounds, use deliberately).

---

## Data design (high level)

### External inputs (from simulator)

- RFQ/BOM via `get_assignment()`.
- Supplier directory via `get_supplier_directory()`.
- Price history via `get_price_history()`.
- Inbox via `list_inbox()`, `read_email()`, `download_attachment()`.
- Sim clock via `get_sim_clock()`.

### Internal state

- **Per-RFQ context:** assignment snapshot, sim clock factor, round id, exam started flag.
- **Per-supplier state:** lifecycle phase, outbound message IDs, last quote extracted (as-sent values), escalation issues raised and approver responses, negotiation history.
- **Dedup registry:** seen email IDs, attachment IDs, processed quote fingerprints.

### Output

- `submit_results` payload per `RFQ_FORMAT.md`.
- **As-sent rule:** line item values reflect what the supplier sent; mismatches handled via `action_taken` and escalation, not by editing numbers. Exception: recomputed `total` / `grand_total` when document arithmetic is wrong.
- **Action precedence:** strongest action per supplier (`escalated` > `answered_question` / `reminded` > `extract`).

### Artifacts (deliverables)

| Artifact | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Loop contract | Goal, boundaries, SOP, stop conditions |
| Code + README | One-command run |
| `submit_results` output | Final quote table |
| `WORKLOG.md` | Append-only human process log |

| Self-evaluation | Honest metrics vs server logs (if required) |

Note: Gergely's 2026-09-18 message lists a shorter deliverable set than the original brief. Include self-eval and screen recording only if still expected; confirm if unsure.

---

## Escalation model (summary only; full rules in spec)

**Must escalate:** missing BOM line, qty mismatch, payment terms mismatch, validity too short, price above history ceiling, negotiation outcome, embedded instructions in supplier content.

**Must not escalate:** arithmetic errors (recompute), duplicate quote (dedupe), silence (remind once), clarifying questions (answer from RFQ).

**Approver protocol:** one issue per email, concrete claim, `[REF:<supplier_id>]` in subject, only after quote is in inbox. After rejection: concrete correction request to supplier, wait for revised quote, re-escalate. Never set `auto_approved: true` until approver actually approved.

---

## Grading mindset

Outcomes matter, not tool choices. An honest 80% self-eval beats a polished 98% claim. Server logs are authoritative for measured metrics. Process quality (transcripts, worklog, loop discipline) is scored separately.

Biggest failure modes to design against:

- LLM decides escalation policy (over-escalation or under-escalation).
- Obeying injection traps in supplier content.
- Editing extracted numbers to "fix" BOM mismatches instead of escalating.
- Escalating before quote exists or with vague claims.
- Double-sending RFQs or reminding too early.
- Burning all 20 dev rounds before the loop is stable.

---

## Risks and open questions

### Resolved from starter pack / FAQ

- MCP URL and env var names.
- Supplier selection: RFQ only to suppliers carrying at least one BOM line.
- Duplicate quote: same quote sent twice, dedupe to one entry.
- Negotiation: state total as plain number in body; outcome always escalates (rule 6).
- No "resend clearer copy" route; extraction gaps are parsing problems, not escalations.
- `request_dev_round()` replaces current round (inbox wiped).

### Still a design decision (not published)

- Silence reminder threshold (think sim-days; too early = penalty).
- Exact poll interval vs sim clock factor.
- Which OpenRouter model for extraction (if used).
- Loop iteration cap for approver rejection cycles.

### Technical risks

- Photo/screenshot extraction quality (highest variance).
- PDFs without reliable text layer.
- As-sent vs recomputed totals edge cases.
- Watermark characters in email bodies (do not strip; use UTF-8).
- Exam unattended for hours: process must be stable, idempotent, restart-safe.

### Administrative

- Confirm exact submission date with Gergely.
- Confirm Cursor transcripts acceptable vs "Claude Code session transcripts" wording.
- Request OpenRouter key when runtime LLM is wired up.

---

## Prior art and references

- Challenge reference videos on loop engineering (linked in brief).
- [Loopany](https://github.com/superdesigndev/loopany) for file-based agent memory patterns (study only).
- [AI-Builder-Club skills](https://github.com/AI-Builder-Club/skills) for verifier and harness patterns (study only).

---

## Repo bootstrap checklist

When creating the implementation repository:

1. Initialize from `python_uv` template.
2. Copy `docs/spec/` from the package (brief, starter pack, sample traffic).
3. Add this `SEED.md`.
4. Produce thin `ARCHITECTURE.md` (project-architecture skill).
5. `anneal init` and define initial changes.
6. Add `WORKLOG.md` (start logging day one).
7. Add `.env.example` with required env var names.
8. Verify MCP connectivity before feature work.
9. First milestone: one `request_dev_round()` processed end-to-end, even with crude extraction.

---

## Non-goals reminder

This is not a product. It is a working miniature of a supplier-quoting system, optimized to pass measured evaluation criteria within a short timebox. Prefer boring, testable, deterministic code over impressive agentic architecture.
